ABSTRACT
Corn straw is the second most produced agricultural residue globally, and the efficient utilization of this resource 
is of great environmental and economic importance. The study utilized Fenton-like reagents for the pretreatment 
of corn straw, followed by carbonization and activation. It was found that the activated carbon samples pre -
treated with Fenton-like reagents exhibited remarkable microporous structures with good electrochemical 
properties. Specifically, activated carbon samples treated with a 0.1 M concentration of FeCl
3

pretreatment resulted in a substantial reduction in greenhouse gas emissions and ecotoxicity in comparison with 
conventional methodologies. The study observed a near 30 % decrease in CO

terrestrial ecotoxicity. This pretreatment method has been demonstrated to enhance activation efficiency while 
concomitantly reducing the amount of activator required. This study demonstrates the potential of Fenton-like 
reagent pretreatment technology in improving the electrochemical performance of activated carbon and 
reducing environmental impact, providing a green and efficient process path.
1. Introduction
Corn straw is the second most produced agricultural residue on a 
global scale. The annual yield of corn straw is 1,661,250 tonnes, rep -
resenting 27.2 % of the total agricultural waste [ 1 – 3 ]. Conventional 
methods of handling maize straw, such as incineration or haphazard 
piling, have been shown to result in a range of environmental issues. 
These include air pollution (e.g., PM2.5, CO
2
) and methane emissions, 
which can trigger eutrophication of water bodies and affect soil micro -
bial communities [ 4 , 5 ]. The carbonization of corn straw to produce 
capacitive carbon materials offers numerous advantages in terms of 
environmental sustainability. Its entire life cycle eco-efficiency is sub -
stantial, making it well-suited to the development of a carbon-neutral 
and circular economy [ 6 , 7 ]. Capacitive carbon materials have a long 
service life in supercapacitors, enabling carbon sequestration for a 
longer period compared to the natural decomposition of straw (1 – 2 
years to release carbon) [ 8 – 12 ].
Corn straw has a widely distributed vascular bundle. The secondary 
cell wall of straw consists of cellulose (which provides the backbone), 
hemicellulose (which connects the cellulose), and lignin (which fills the 
cross-links) to form a dense composite system. When the straw is used 
for high-capacitance activated carbon, the denseness of the secondary 
wall hinders the diffusion of the activator, resulting in an uneven dis -
tribution of pores that affects subsequent activation processes [ 13 , 14 ]. 
Consequently, activators that are more than 2 – 3 times the mass of the 
feedstock are employed to activate high-performance activated carbon 
materials using conventional process methods [ 15 , 16 ]. In this study, 
Fenton-like reagent pretreatment was employed to minimize the quan -
tity of activator during the fabrication of high-performance activated 
carbon materials.
Fenton reagents and their analogues (Fenton-like) represent a class 
of advanced oxidation technologies grounded in the utilization of hy -

The concept of Fenton ’ s reagent is utilized to deliberately disrupt the 
structural integrity of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin in plants. 
Reference is made to the lignin dimer model in Fig. 1 to simulate the 
behavior of treatment with the Fenton-like reagent. It is predicted that 
this process will weaken the plant structure and result in the formation 
of fine plant tissues [ 24 , 25 ]. This is anticipated to ease the subsequent 
carbonization and activation steps, which may allow for a reduced 
quantity of KOH to be utilized as an activator in order to achieve the 
desired outcomes. Additionally, this approach could be developed into a 
more environmentally friendly pretreatment technology. The reduced 
quantity of activator employed in this method leads to an increased 
reliance on ferric chloride and hydrogen peroxide. As a result, there is a 
need for a more comprehensive evaluation method — specifically, a life 
cycle assessment — to scientifically ascertain its environmental impact.
Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is a methodology that is employed to 
determine the most sustainable approach by considering various envi -
ronmental impact parameters. Consequently, the incorporation of such 
evaluations into biochar production studies is strongly suggested to 
accurately assess its energy-saving and emission-reduction benefits, as 
previously proposed by 
¨
Ogmundarson et al. and Yu et al. [ 26 , 27 ]. In 
recent years, there has been a gradual increase in the number of studies 
related to analyzing biomass energy storage applications using whole 
life cycle assessment. Kulkarni et al. [ 28 ]. found that the environmental 
impacts of the production of battery-grade graphite from biomass as a 
precursor using an electrochemical graphitization process were lower 
than those of conventional methods. Antic Gorrazzi et al. [ 29 ]. investi -
gated the potential of Cyperus papyrus biochar as an electrode material. 
Their findings demonstrated that, despite electrical conductivity and 
mechanical strength limitations, low-temperature biochar has a signif -
icantly lower carbon footprint than graphite. These studies highlight the 
crucial role of Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) in identifying sustainable 
pathways for biochar production. They also illustrate the potential of 
biochar to minimize environmental impact and serve as a feasible 
alternative to conventional graphite in energy storage applications.
In this study, activated carbon was prepared using Fenton-like re -
agent pretreatment to evaluate its performance as a capacitive material. 
A life cycle assessment was conducted to determine whether this method 
qualifies as a green treatment technology.

2.3. Life cycle assessment (LCA)
The study adhered to the guidelines established by the international 
environmental standards “ ISO 14040: Principles and Framework ” and 
“ ISO 14044: Requirements and Guidelines ” (International Organization 
for Standardization, 2006). The Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) was con -
ducted in four stages: first, the goal and scope were defined, followed by 
Life Cycle Inventory Analysis (LCI), then Life Cycle Impact Assessment 
(LCIA), and finally, the Interpretation of results.
2.3.1. Goal and scope definition
The present study focuses on the environmental impact assessment of 
the production of 1 kg of activated carbon, utilizing a Cradle-to-Gate 
(CTG) system boundary. This boundary encompasses the acquisition of 
feedstock, its transportation, the production process (including the 
carbonization and activation stages), and the associated energy con -
sumption. As illustrated in Table 1 , the LCA study encompasses three 
distinct scenarios, distinguished by variations in pretreatment method -
ology, activation parameters, and activator dosage. The system bound -
aries of the three scenarios targeted in the study are illustrated in Fig. 2 . 
As demonstrated, the process commences at the origin of corn straw 
(corn cultivation) and culminates with the yield of the product (1 kg of 
activated carbon).
2.3.2. Life cycle inventory (LCI)
In this study, the life cycle inventory (LCI) was created using the 
Ecoinvent 3.9.1 database integrated into OpenLCA software. The in -
ventory data was mainly sourced from both domestic and international 
literature. Typical or average values, common energy consumption 
figures, and reasonable projections based on the calorific value and 
utilization rate of fuels were selected. The Ecoinvent 3.9.1 database is 
lacking data concerning ferric chloride production and emission. 
Consequently, the information on ferric chloride production and emis -
sion in this study was referred to the research results of Dodbiba et al. 
[ 30 ]. Except for data related to ferric chloride, upstream information on 
the other chemicals in the study is included in the database. Based on the 
data from Ref. [ 31 ], who evaluated the construction, operation, and 
maintenance of biomass pyrolysis plants in China, this life cycle in -
ventory considers a scale of 1000 t/a for biochar production. For the 
production of 1 ton of straw biochar, 23.62 kg of bricks, 0.0072 m
3 
of 
concrete, and 1.07 kg of steel are required. During the pyrolysis and 
product treatment process, 1 ton of field straw biomass feedstock re -
quires 205.47 kWh of electricity and 272,040 kg of tap water annually 
[ 32 ].
2.3.3. Life cycle impact assessment (LCIA)
In this process, the assessment involves converting input and output 
data into indicators relevant to each impact category. The current study 
utilized the ReCiPe 2016 Interim (H) methodology for Life Cycle 
Assessment (LCIA). The ReCiPe 2016 Interim (H) methodology was 
selected for LCIA due to its comprehensive coverage of environmental 
impact categories (including ecotoxicity, eutrophication, global warm -
ing potential, and resource depletion) and wide acceptance in biomass 
conversion and sustainable materials research [ 26 , 27 ]. This methodol -
ogy enables quantitative comparison of multi-dimensional environ -
mental impacts, which is critical for evaluating the green attributes of 
the proposed pretreatment technology.
2.3.4. Interpretation of results
The conclusions and recommendations are derived from the outcome 
assessment of the LCIA phase. The results have undergone meticulous 
analysis, with consideration given to the objectives and scope of the 
study, while taking into account the limitations of the data and meth -
odology. By identifying potential environmental impacts throughout the

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Characterization of the activated carbon
The activated carbon derived from corn straw was analyzed using 
scanning electron microscopy. As shown in Fig. 3 , the activated carbon 
samples obtained through Fenton-like pretreatment retained the orig -
inal three-dimensional structure of the straw after the activation pro -
cess. As the concentration of Fenton-like reagent increases, structural 
reorganization of the material can be observed via SEM images. 
Comprehensive observation shows that CSFTAC-0.1 ( Fig. 3 B) exhibits a 
more refined layered porous structure. The mesoporous structures of 
CSFTAC-0.1 are essential for facilitating ion transport during electro -
chemical processes [ 33 ].
The prepared activated carbon was further analyzed using nitrogen 
adsorption-desorption at 77 K, as shown in Fig. 4 b. The nitrogen 
adsorption of CSFTAC-0.1 exhibited a notable increase at relatively low- 
pressure levels (p/p < 0.01). The isotherms displayed a type I adsorption 
behavior without hysteresis loops, indicating that the activated carbon 
derived from corn straw contains a significant amount of micropores. As 
the concentration of the Fenton reagent increased, the specific surface 
area of the activated carbon (CSFTAC) initially increased and then 
decreased. The higher concentration of Fe
3 +
likely promoted the

scan rate of 20 mV s
� 1

rectangular curves, with CSAC-2 showing a more pronounced redox 
peak, likely due to a higher content of oxygen-containing functional

Despite the relatively limited surface area of the micropores, the use

. Combined with the 
preceding XPS analysis ( Fig. S1 and S2 ), which revealed no detectable Fe 
signal, this further confirms that iron species are present in a highly 
dispersed, low-loading state within the material. This low-loading 
feature offers key insights into the dominant mechanism underlying 
the investigated electrochemical performance. The exceptional specific 
capacitance of the CSFTAC series samples is primarily derived from 
double-layer capacitance and pseudo capacitance, originating from the 
high specific surface area, well-developed pore structure, and abundant 
oxygen-containing functional groups optimized via Fenton pretreat -
ment. The faint redox peaks observed in the CV curves, upon analysis, do 
not align with the characteristic potential of iron species; instead, they 
are more likely derived from the abundant reversible quinone/phenol 
redox pairs on the material surface. Thus, the presence of trace iron is 
not the primary driver of the electrode material ’ s high performance, and 
its electrochemical contribution is far less significant than the structural 
optimization of the carbon matrix induced by the pretreatment.
The curve in Fig. 6 f depicts the Nyquist plot. The curves display a 
slight semicircular pattern in the high-frequency region and a linear 
trend in the low-frequency region. A reduction in the semicircular 
diameter indicates a decrease in charge transfer resistance (Rct), while 
an increase in the slope of the linear segment signifies a decrease in 
diffusion resistance (Warburg impedance, W). The slope of the linear 
portion can be utilized to characterize diffusion resistance, and Fig. 6 f 
demonstrates a clear correlation between the slope and the electro -
chemical properties of the material. The reduction in diffusion resistance 
is attributed to the increased slope of the linear segment in the low- 
frequency region. Consequently, the performance of CSFTAC-0.1 is 
significantly enhanced compared to the CSAC-1 material.

during the preparation of activated carbon by directly mixing biomass

4. Conclusion
The main conclusions of this work are as follows: 
(1). This enhancement has been demonstrated to have a substantial 
impact on performance metrics. Corn stalks that had been pre -
treated with a Fenton-like reagent were found to yield activated 
carbon with an ideal hierarchical porous structure and high 
specific surface area (1842 m
2
/g). This material exhibits 
remarkable electrochemical performance, with a specific capac -
itance reaching 342 F g
� 1 
at a current density of 0.5 A g
� 1 
and 
maintaining 238 F g
� 1 
even at the high current density of 20 A 
g
� 1
, outperforming most biomass-derived carbon electrodes.
(2). Noteworthy environmental advantages: When combined with life 
cycle assessment results, this pretreatment method is not only 
highly efficient and straightforward but also an environmentally 
friendly process. In comparison with the conventional two-step 
process, its terrestrial ecotoxicity potential is reduced by 59.1 
% (to 45.86 kg 1,4-DCB-Eq); in comparison with the conventional 
one-step process, its global warming potential is reduced by 29.4 
% (a decrease of 2.30 kg CO
2
-Eq, to 5.54 kg CO
2
-Eq), 
demonstrating clear advantages in reducing toxicity and miti -
gating climate change.
(3). The technical advantages and mechanisms are as follows: This 
pretreatment effectively promotes the development of micro -
pores and mesopores during subsequent carbonization, while 
significantly enhancing activator efficiency. This process has 
been shown to enhance the final pore structure of activated 
carbon.
Despite the ecological and economic advantages of this pretreatment 
technology, our preliminary studies suggest that the efficacy of the 
treatment on nut-shell biomass is suboptimal when such reagents are 
employed. Subsequent research endeavors should employ life-cycle cost 
analysis to validate the economic viability of this enhanced approach.
